objective: An audit of Relay's Loop Engine found four related latent defects in three of its gates, each of which says more than it knows. All are in pure modules under `src/relay/mission/loop/` whose own headers state the rule they break. Fix all four, in place, without changing anything else. (A) COMPLETION. `evaluateLoopCompletion` (`loop-completion.ts`) documents that "a Loop whose only shortfall is trust returns `claimed_complete`, not `incomplete`", but the test it uses for that (`onlyTrustIsMissing`) ignores the mission verdict, the independent review and the durability of the terminal write, so a Loop is reported as a mere claim when a fact about the work itself failed. (D) NOTHING SUPPORTS COMPLETION. The same module's header says "a `claim` can never, on its own, end a Loop", and `COMPLETION_SUPPORTING_TRUSTS` excludes `observed` as well; but when a Loop has no blocking criteria its trust check is vacuously satisfied, so a Loop whose evidence is only claims or observations, or that has no evidence at all, can be reported `verified_complete`. (B) PAUSE THRESHOLD. `authorizeScheduledSpend` (`cron/cron-budget.ts`) compares spend to the automatic pause fraction in whole parts per million, but its conversion of the fraction can move the threshold UP, so a schedule keeps spending past the point it was told to pause — the fail-open the module's own comments say review already removed once; and its configuration guard, which says a fraction below one part per million is refused, accepts some of them. (C) INSTANTS. `readIsoInstantWithOffset` (`runtime/loop-scheduler.ts`) is the ONE reader of offset-carrying ISO-8601 instants that the scheduler and the cron modules import. It checks the text's shape with a regular expression and then hands it to `Date.parse`, which rolls a calendar date that does not exist forward to a later real day, so a recurring approval grant whose expiry names such a day authorizes an operation after the date it named, and a run stamped on such a day is planned as though the stamp were readable. `seed/src/relay/loop-fixes.test.ts` is already written and currently fails; it pins the main behaviours of each fix and deliberately not every wider invariant. The files to edit exist and are tracked by git: edit them in place.
requirements: A. `evaluateLoopCompletion` returns `claimed_complete` only when the trust check (`blocking criteria supported by attested or verified evidence`) failed and nothing that is a FACT ABOUT THE WORK failed: no unconfirmable iteration, no open blocking finding, an acceptable mission verdict (below), no review that ran and did not approve, and a durable terminal write. Otherwise a Loop that is not verified_complete is `incomplete`. THE MISSION VERDICT comes from Relay's mission verdict engine, which is NOT in this workspace and which you cannot read; its values mean: `verified_complete` every blocking requirement is satisfied with Relay-produced evidence; `approved` a reviewer approved but verification is incomplete; `reviewed` a review occurred, approval and verification are not complete; `claimed_complete` the implementer reported completion, a claim, not evidence; `partially_complete` work in progress; `blocked` open blocking findings, exceeded repair or review limits, or a cancelled run; `failed` the run failed; `needs_human` a checkpoint needs a human decision; `null` Unknown. `failed`, `blocked`, `needs_human`, `partially_complete` and `null` are always facts about the work. Two cases are a genuine design choice; either answer is acceptable, applied consistently and stated in a code comment: (1) whether a REQUIRED review that has NOT RUN yet, or that APPROVED but was NOT structurally independent, is missing corroboration (so `claimed_complete` remains possible) or a failed requirement (`incomplete`); (2) whether the unverified rungs of the verdict ladder (`approved` above `reviewed` above `claimed_complete`) are trust shortfalls: none of them, or a top segment of the ladder (`approved`; `approved` and `reviewed`; or all three), so a rung counts only if every rung above it counts. A review that RAN and did not approve is never a trust shortfall, whether or not the reviewer was independent: it is a hard failure. When the trust check PASSES (every blocking criterion is supported), a mission verdict other than `verified_complete` makes the Loop `incomplete` under every choice (the repository's own tests pin `claimed_complete` there as incomplete): `claimed_complete` is reachable only when the trust check failed. When no review is required, the review flags (all false) play no part. `reasons` carries exactly one entry per failing check (that check's own detail), in check order, as today: a Loop with one failing check reports one reason, a Loop with two reports two. A CONSEQUENCE TO BE AWARE OF, NOT TO FIX: the production engine that calls this function (not in this workspace) always passes `reviewOccurred`, `reviewApproved` and `reviewerWasIndependent` as false and sets `independentReviewRequired` whenever a reviewer is configured, so under the strict answer to choice (1) `claimed_complete` is unreachable in production whenever a reviewer is configured; both answers remain acceptable. The `checks`, `reasons` and `unsupportedBlockingCriterionIds` it reports, and the `verified_complete` path, are unchanged except as D requires.

D. A Loop with no blocking acceptance criterion (none at all, or only non-blocking ones) whose evidence has nothing at `attested` or `verified` (only `claim` or `observed` evidence, or none) is never `verified_complete`, and its result carries at least one reason saying why. Design choice, either acceptable, stated in a code comment: (a) this is a trust shortfall: `claimed_complete` when nothing else fails, `incomplete` when something else does; or (b) a Loop with no blocking criterion is not completable at all: `incomplete`, whatever its evidence, attested included. Whichever answer is chosen, the verdict is the SAME for zero evidence, claim-only evidence and observed-only evidence, and the same for an empty criteria list and a list of only non-blocking criteria: one shortfall, one verdict. A Loop with at least one blocking criterion is unaffected by this fix.

B. `authorizeScheduledSpend` never applies the pause threshold LATER than configured. Read the configured fraction f (0 < f <= 1) as the decimal it is written as (its shortest round-trip form, as JavaScript prints it): a window whose spent/cap is at or above that decimal is never authorized. When f has at most six decimal places (a whole number of parts per million) the comparison is EXACT: it pauses at spent/cap = f and does not pause one part per million below it. For a finer fraction the decision may pause at most one part per million EARLY, or the fraction may be refused as `invalid_budget_configuration`; either is acceptable. A fraction below one part per million stays refused as configuration (the repository's own test pins 0.0000004), and no fraction ever makes a window with a positive cap that has spent nothing reach the pause threshold. A ZERO CAP's behaviour is UNCHANGED: with a cap of zero the window reports `cap_exceeded` and, when a pause fraction is configured, `auto_pause_threshold_reached` beside it, exactly as today. The comparison stays exact integer (BigInt) arithmetic on the micros, for any number of micros; every other check, refusal reason, detail sentence and the headroom are unchanged. Correcting the comments in `cron-budget.ts` that speak of permille where the denominator is parts per million is IN SCOPE as part of this fix (it is not an unrelated cleanup).

C. `readIsoInstantWithOffset` returns `null` for a text whose calendar date does not exist in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, including years 0000-0099 (0000 is a leap year; a century year is a leap year only when divisible by 400), judged on the date AS WRITTEN, in the text's own offset, not on the UTC date it would parse to. Every instant that exists reads exactly as it does today (the same epoch milliseconds as `Date.parse`), EXCEPT the T24:00 literal below; that includes leap days, month ends, nine-digit fractions and offsets that carry the instant across midnight; everything it refuses today stays refused. THE T24:00 LITERAL is a genuine design choice: every spelling of hour 24 that `Date.parse` accepts today (`T24:00`, `T24:00:00`, and `T24:00:00` with an all-zero fraction such as `T24:00:00.000`; all of them currently read as the next day's 00:00) is either refused, or kept as that next-day midnight; one way for all of them, stated in a code comment. Fix it in this one shared reader, not in its callers. Its callers: in this workspace `cron-approvals.ts` (read-only; the operation instant and grant expiries) and `planLoopPass` (last-advanced stamps); outside this workspace `cron-missed.ts` (the evaluation instant and occurrence instants), `cron-occurrences.ts` (window bounds), `cron-tick.ts` (the evaluation instant and window end) and `cron-versioning.ts` (a proposed version's `authoredAt`). Each then refuses such a text by the reason it already has.

No function outside these four fixes changes behaviour, including `planLoopPass` beyond what the reader's fix implies, `trustSupportsCompletion`, `claimAloneCompletes`, the spend windows, the reviewer reservation, the concurrency and guard checks, and every exported name and type. `cron-approvals.ts` is read-only: it is one of the reader's consumers, and the specification runs against it.

acceptanceCriteria.text: `claimed_complete` is returned only when the trust check failed and no fact about the work failed (unconfirmable iteration, open blocking finding, a failed, blocked, needs-human, partial or Unknown mission verdict, a review that ran and did not approve whether or not independent, an undurable terminal write); with the trust check passing, any mission verdict short of verified_complete is incomplete; the two stated design choices (an unrun or non-independent approving review; which top segment of the approved/reviewed/claimed_complete ladder counts as trust) are each answered one way, consistently, and stated in a comment; a Loop that needs no review is unaffected by the review flags; checks, reasons, unsupported ids and the verified path are unchanged except as D requires.

With no blocking criterion and nothing at attested or verified, a Loop is never verified_complete and its result gives at least one reason; the verdict is the same for zero, claim-only and observed-only evidence and for no criteria or only non-blocking ones; the chosen answer (claimed_complete as a trust shortfall, or not completable) is applied consistently and stated in a comment; a Loop with blocking criteria is unaffected.

The pause threshold is never applied later than the fraction as written; a six-decimal fraction compares exactly (pauses at it, not one part per million below it); a finer fraction pauses at most one part per million early or is refused as configuration; a fraction below one part per million is refused; a zero-spend window with a positive cap never reaches the threshold, and a zero cap behaves exactly as today; arithmetic on micros stays exact BigInt at any magnitude; every other refusal and the headroom are unchanged.

`readIsoInstantWithOffset` refuses every calendar date that does not exist, judged as written in its own offset (Gregorian leap years, centuries and years 0000-0099 included), reads every existing instant to the same milliseconds as before except the T24:00 literal (offsets crossing midnight, fractions, month ends included), keeps every existing refusal, handles every spelling of T24:00 one stated way, and is fixed in the shared reader so every caller inherits it through its existing refusal reasons.

Only `loop-completion.ts`, `cron-budget.ts` and `loop-scheduler.ts` are changed, using no new dependency or import; `cron-approvals.ts` is untouched; no exported name, signature or type changes; inputs are not mutated; no unrelated reformatting.
